summary: Sets out the IETF's policies on intellectual property rights such as patents in technologies it develops, and the goals of those policies. The aim is that participants know about IPR constraints early. It replaces RFC 3979 and RFC 4879 and updates RFC 2026.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a group builds something together, everyone should tell the others if they own any ideas in it. These are the rules for that.

questions: do ietf participants have to disclose patents
subtitle: Who must tell the IETF about patents, when, and how, so working groups can choose technology with open eyes.

tldr.problem: A working group choosing between technical proposals needs to know early about any patent or similar claims that might cover them, but the IETF cannot judge whether such claims are valid.
tldr.mechanism: Contributors and other participants must disclose IPR they reasonably and personally know covers a Contribution, as soon as reasonably possible, using the IETF's public disclosure process, with optional licensing terms that become irrevocable.
tldr.outcome: Working groups weigh disclosed IPR and licensing terms alongside technical merit, with no official preference among license types. The memo is BCP 79 and obsoletes RFC 3979 and RFC 4879.

facts.label: Update verification
facts.value: Three separate inquiries and at least 30 days

today: RFC 8179 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 79) published in May 2017, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It replaced RFC 3979 and RFC 4879; the companion policy on copyright and similar rights is RFC 5378.

sections.title: Goals and Three Basic Principles
sections.content:
The IETF policy on Intellectual Property Rights (IPR), such as patent rights, is designed so that working groups and participants have as much information as possible about IPR constraints on a technical proposal as early as possible. RFC 8179 (BCP 79) updates RFC 2026, with RFC 5378 replaces Section 10 of it, and obsoletes RFC 3979 and RFC 4879.

Three principles, originally from RFC 2026, underpin it:

  • The IETF makes no determination about the validity of any particular IPR claim.
  • The IETF, following normal processes, can decide to use technology for which IPR disclosures have been made if it decides that use is warranted.
  • Everyone contributing to a working group must disclose IPR that they or any other participant believe covers or may ultimately cover the technology under discussion. This covers IPR of the participant, their employer, sponsor or others they represent that is reasonably and personally known. No patent search is required.

Copyrights and trademarks in Contributions are dealt with separately in RFC 5378. The memo is not legal advice.
sections.plainLanguage: The team does not decide who is right about who owns an idea. It just wants everyone to say early if they own one, so the team can choose wisely.

sections.title: Key Definitions
sections.content:
IPR means a patent, utility model or similar right that may Cover an Implementing Technology, anywhere in the world, including registrations, renewals and applications. A claim Covers a technology when a valid claim of a patent or patent application (including a provisional application) would necessarily be infringed by exercising a right with respect to it. An Implementing Technology is a technology that implements an IETF specification or standard.

A Contribution is a submission meant for an Internet-Draft or RFC, or a statement in an IETF activity, that is intended to affect the IETF Standards Process or relates to an Alternate Stream that has adopted the policy. It may be oral or written, and written covers email, slides, chat and discussion board postings. Invited background presentations are often not Contributions. A Participant is anyone acting to influence an IETF discussion; a Working Group Chair or Area Director is Participating in all activities of their groups.

Reasonably and personally known means what a person knows personally or would be expected to know because of their job. It does not require a patent search. An Alternate Stream is the IAB, IRTF or Independent Submission stream, or any future non-IETF stream.
sections.plainLanguage: A patent is a claim that only the owner may build a certain invention. Reasonably known means what you know or should know from your own job, with no need to go hunting for hidden ones.

sections.title: Who Must Disclose and What Happens If They Do Not
sections.content:
Taking part in the IETF means being deemed to comply with this RFC. Three groups are involved. A Contributor who reasonably and personally knows of IPR that they believe Covers or may ultimately Cover their written Contribution, or that their employer or sponsor may assert against implementations of it, must disclose. A Participant who knows of such IPR relating to someone else's written Contribution must also disclose. Anyone else is encouraged to make a voluntary disclosure, for example for third party IPR.

The duty applies to IPR that the person or their employer or sponsor owns, can license or assert, derives pecuniary benefit from, or on which the person is listed as an inventor. An obligation is also satisfied if the IPR owner, such as the employer, makes the disclosure instead. For oral Contributions the Contributor must give an oral declaration or file a disclosure.

A person who cannot or will not disclose must not contribute to or participate in IETF activities on technologies they know may be Covered by undisclosed IPR, unless they know their employer or sponsor will disclose on their behalf. Participating without making required disclosures is a violation of IETF policy, and sanctions are available through the normal IETF processes, as summarized in RFC 6701.
sections.plainLanguage: If you know that you or your boss own an idea the team is about to use, you must say so. If you cannot say so, you should stay out of that part of the project.

sections.title: Making, Timing and Updating a Disclosure
sections.content:
A disclosure must be made as soon as reasonably possible after the Contribution is submitted, or after the person first learns of the IPR if that comes later. Participants who realize IPR may cover technology being seriously discussed are strongly encouraged to make a preliminary disclosure before a Contribution is even made. Area Directors who see Contributions late in the process cannot be expected to disclose before they become aware of them.

Disclosures follow the instructions at the IETF web site and must not appear in RFCs or other Contributions; the RFC Editor removes IPR-related information before publication. A disclosure must include, to the extent reasonably available, patent or application numbers, inventor names, the specific IETF Document or activity affected, and the Internet-Draft version if relevant.

A disclosure must be updated promptly when an unpublished application is published, an application is abandoned, a patent issues on a disclosed application, or a material change to the document brings in additional IPR. Disclosures are assumed to be inherited by later revisions and by the resulting RFCs. If someone other than the original submitter proposes an update, the Secretariat tries to verify it with the submitter, with three separate inquiries and at least 30 days before falling back to evidence of control of the IPR.

A blanket statement that IPR may exist on every Contribution does not satisfy the requirement. A commitment to license all of one's relevant IPR to implementers royalty-free, and otherwise reasonably and non-discriminatorily, with other terms disclosed, does.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the team as soon as you know, in the official place, not buried inside the project paper. If things change, like a pending idea getting approved, you update what you said.

sections.title: Licensing Information and Its Binding Effect
sections.content:
Including a licensing declaration is not mandatory but is encouraged, because working groups use it when comparing options. It is helpful to say whether, once the IESG approves the specification as an RFC, all persons can implement it under a) a royalty-free and otherwise reasonable and non-discriminatory license, b) a reasonable and non-discriminatory license that may include a reasonable royalty, or c) without needing a license, for example under a covenant not to sue.

Once a disclosure includes licensing declarations or similar information, the discloser agrees these are irrevocable and attach, to the extent permitted by law, to the IPR. Implementers may rely on them even if the IPR is transferred, and the holder must ensure the commitments bind any transferee. The IETF Secretariat may ask the IPR holder for a written assurance of one of the license options. The result does not itself block publication or advancement of a document, though a working group may weigh it and the IESG may defer approval to help obtain assurances.
sections.plainLanguage: If an owner promises how others may use their idea, the promise sticks, even if the idea is later sold to someone else.

sections.title: How Working Groups Weigh IPR
sections.content:
Working groups generally prefer technologies with no known IPR claims or an offer of royalty-free licensing, but they have discretion to adopt a patented technology if it is superior enough to outweigh the cost. The IETF has no official preference among license terms. The RFC offers informational observations on common conditions: fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory terms that may bear royalties (FRAND or RAND), royalty-free terms (RAND-z), and commitments not to assert, possibly conditional on reciprocity. Open source projects often prefer the latter two.

Level of use matters: for a mandatory-to-implement change to a widely deployed protocol, the hurdle for encumbered technologies should be very high. An IETF consensus says no mandatory-to-implement security technology can be specified unless it has no known IPR claims or a royalty-free license is available, unless there is a very good, documented reason agreed by IETF consensus.

The absence of disclosures today does not mean none will come later, and a disclosure does not show the IPR is valid, enforceable or actually Covers the Contribution. The IESG will not decide whether licensing terms were fulfilled in practice; it applies the normal requirements for advancing standards (see RFC 6410).
sections.plainLanguage: The team likes ideas that are free to use, but may pick one with a price tag if it is much better. For something every device must use, the team is extra picky.

sections.title: Change Control, Advancement and Other Streams
sections.content:
The IETF must have change control over the technology in Standards Track documents so it can fix problems or produce derivative works. A developer of controlled technology may hand change control to the IETF, which can be complex (RFC 1790 and RFC 2339 are examples). A Standards Track document may still normatively reference proprietary technology, for instance proprietary cryptographic transforms.

To advance a standard, RFC 6410 requires implementations to show at least two independent, separate and successful uses of the licensing process when the technology requires patented or controlled technology. The key word is requires: disclosed IPR does not necessarily mean a license is needed.

IETF Documents must not mention specific IPR; readers are pointed to the IETF's online IPR list. The rules apply to the IETF stream. Managers of Alternate Streams may publicly adopt them for their own streams. The Security Considerations section says there are no known security issues with IPR procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: Even if someone owns an idea, the team needs to be able to fix and update the finished thing. The rules apply to this team's work, and other teams may choose to copy them.

sections.title: What Changed Since RFC 3979 and RFC 4879
sections.content:
Section 13 reviews the content changes from RFC 3979 and is informational only; the text of Sections 1 to 12 prevails. Boilerplate was deleted because it has moved to the Trust Legal Provisions.

New definitions include Alternate Stream and Participating in an IETF discussion or activity. Contribution now requires that a statement be intended to affect the IETF Standards Process, so informational presentations such as guest speakers are not Contributions, and it now lists BOFs, design teams, web sites and chat rooms. Covers now includes provisional patent applications. The IPR definition no longer refers to copyrights, database rights and data rights, since copyright is handled in RFC 5378.
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook was cleaned up so that its words are clearer about who counts as taking part and which kinds of ideas it covers.

items.title: No validity ruling
items.text: The IETF makes no determination about the validity of any IPR claim.

items.title: Use is allowed
items.text: The IETF can use technology with IPR disclosures if it decides that is warranted.

items.title: Disclose what you know
items.text: Contributors and other participants disclose IPR they believe covers the technology. No patent search is required.

viz.caption: LICENSING OPTIONS A DISCLOSURE MAY STATE (SECTION 5.5.A)

items.label: Royalty-free
items.desc: Royalty-free and otherwise reasonable and non-discriminatory license.

items.label: Reasonable terms
items.desc: Reasonable and non-discriminatory terms, including a reasonable royalty or other payment.

items.label: No license needed
items.desc: Rights obtainable without a license, for example a covenant not to sue.

cells: Fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory terms that may bear royalties or other financial obligations.
Royalty-free terms that are otherwise fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory.
Commitment not to assert declared IPR, possibly conditional on reciprocity.
